title: The tech helping crack decades-old cold cases
text:
Randy Gail Sperino was last seen alive on the evening of 9 November 1993, as she was getting into a pickup truck in Granite City, Illinois.

The 34-year-old's body was found hours later in a field nearby, the victim of blunt force trauma.

The identity of her killer was a mystery. DNA evidence found at the crime scene was tested against standard law enforcement databases, but no matches were found.

For three decades, investigators from the Madison County Sheriff's Office chased leads and interviewed hundreds of people as they attempted to identify the perpetrator.

The case looked like it would remain one of more than 250,000 unsolved homicides in the US.

Then, last year, detectives tried a fresh approach. They sent genetic evidence to Othram, a Houston-based company that uses DNA technology to help identify the perpetrators in cold and current crime cases.

The Madison County detectives had been inspired by investigative genetic genealogy techniques used to identify the Golden State Killer, Joseph James DeAngelo, back in 2018. In that case, an investigative team constructed a family tree to help identify the killer.

They were able to do so thanks to DNA data that relatives had provided to commercial databases, similar to consumer ancestry platforms.

Unlike traditional forensic DNA testing, which generally relies on a direct comparison between evidence and a known person, investigative genetic genealogy can identify distant genetic relatives of an unknown individual.

Othram set about applying this technique to track down Sperino's killer. While the killer's own DNA profile wasn't available, profiles submitted by his extended relatives allowed the company to identify a male family member.

"That lead broke the case open," said Captain Tim Lawrence of Madison County Sheriff's Office, which was responsible for investigating the crime.

It was a crucial clue that led the detectives to Albert "Buddy" Zigler, 70, who then confessed to the murder. He was charged in May this year.

Wes Sperino, Gail's son, said at a press conference: "I finally get closure and I finally know who did this."

The technique that led detectives to Zigler is credited with revolutionising how forensic cases are solved.

It has been highly successful in helping solve cases involving unidentified human remains and identifying suspects in longstanding investigations.

Othram claims it has helped solve thousands of cases. The company's chief executive David Mittelman likens investigative genetic genealogy to a GPS system: "The DNA profile is the GPS signal and it says 'you belong here.' But to understand where 'here' is, you need a map."

Public records, obituaries, and census data build that map so Othram's scientists can establish how different family trees connect.

However, Mittelman is quick to point out that DNA technology can only go so far before "a cascade of investigative steps" are needed.

DNA science isn't the only technology that are helping detectives solve cold cases.

One of the challenges facing detectives on major cases investigations like the hunt for Sperino's killer is the sheer amount of evidence they dig up.

Officers investigating Sperino's murder realised AI could help them wade through the mountains of evidence they had accumulated since 1993.

They used a platform called Centerline AI, from Florida software company CentralSquare, to analyse more than 2,000 pages of records and identify evidence for the DNA testing that helped to break the case.

The AI helped them reconstruct timelines and organise witness information. "It's so much easier than having a detective have to read through 2,000 pages," Lawrence says. His team could interact with the AI like a chat bot.

This also helped when it came to interviewing Zigler after they had tracked him down. Detectives were able to ask questions of the AI to help "figure out if Zigler was being truthful", says Lawrence.

But the technology is "only as good as the investigator," says the captain. There comes a point, he says, "where you leave the technology behind and you have to go track people down and talk to them."

Investigative genetic genealogy has its limitations too. Mittelman says: "It can't solve every case. If you have no DNA, you can't really use this technique."

"But this technique is a lot more powerful and a lot more likely to yield identities than having to rely on the chance that you find a match somewhere in a database," he adds.

While firms like Othram only use ancestry platforms where users have provided consent for law enforcement matching, there remain some concerns about the ethical implications of using this data.

"There are significant privacy concerns," says Denise Syndercombe Court, professor of forensic genetics at King's College London. While one person may have opted in to their DNA being used, genetic relatives may not have given consent.

A lack of funding is another hurdle. Mittelman says: "Every law enforcement agency wants to do it. There's just not a lot of funding for it."

Sometimes cases are funded through donations or crowdfunding. Othram operates a website listing cases that members of the public can help fund.

While investigative genetic genealogy has been adopted in countries such as Sweden, Denmark and Australia, it is not yet used in the UK. The Home Office is conducting a study to consider whether it should be adopted in the UK but did not respond to a request for comment.

The UK is already in a strong position, says Syndercombe Court. "We have such an efficient DNA database that if you can get any DNA out of a crime scene, you've got over a 65% chance of putting a name to that person, which is enormously powerful," she says.

title: Garmin Brings Voice Control to Your Handlebars with the New Edge 1060
author: Josh Ross
text:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Garmin just dropped a three-pronged update to the brand’s cycling portfolio with new options for both the front of your bike and your winter riding. The launch includes the new flagship bike computer, the Garmin Edge 1060, along with the Edge Explore 3 and Edge Explore 3 Plus that offer recreational cyclists and e-bike riders a more affordable option. The announcement also covers a new and more affordable indoor trainer called the Tacx Nēra, which offers similar movement as the Garmin Tacx Neo 3M for half the price. Here’s what each announcement brings to the table and why you might want to care, or not, about the latest Garmin news.

Two years ago, the Garmin Edge 1050 launched, and it marked a drastic right turn for the Garmin Edge series strategy. While the previous x40 generation (540/840/1040) had solar options and incredible battery life, they also had slower processors and dimmer screens. Clearly, some market analysis had taken place at Garmin because the Edge 1050 launched with half the battery life of the previous flagship Edge 1040 Solar, but also brought one of the best screens on the market with it. Suddenly you had a lot less battery life, but the form factor was sleek and the screen was both bright and noticeably higher resolution. Some people, myself included, initially mourned the loss, but most people seemed to appreciate how gorgeous the screen actually was, and 20 hours (on the flagship 1050) really is pretty good. There’s also a battery saver mode that pushes it to 60 hours when you absolutely must have the battery life.

Now the Edge 1060 is hitting the market at $799.99, and it looks a lot more like an Edge 1050 Plus than a truly new generation. The new computer refines what works and adds new features that feel like natural extensions of the strategy that Garmin is currently executing. The headline of those features is surely the microphone.

Voice control was what you were hoping for, right? The new Garmin Edge 1060 adds a built-in microphone powering Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and allowing for “Okay, Garmin” functionality. Like a smartphone, you can keep your hands on the bar and talking to your computer lets you request ride data, pull up new routes, or report road hazards. The microphone also integrates directly with the Garmin Messenger app, allowing you to send voice messages hands-free.

The other major update to the Edge 1060 is the packaging. The Edge 1050 was one of a new generation of larger bike computers, but it was also relatively lightweight. It meant that not every single out-front mount had to be completely redesigned, but some did, and according to K-Edge, the weight of a bike computer actually matters a lot when you start trying to hang lights under it. The Edge 1060 is a genuine improvement here, offering a 19-gram weight reduction, dropping from 161g down to 142g. Likely more important to more people, though, the outer dimensions have also been reduced. The 1060 shrinks its overall footprint by over a centimeter in length (106.9mm down from 118.5mm) and it’s narrower by about 2mm. That will help with tight fitment on some out-front mounts—I’m looking at you, Specialized—but since Garmin is using the exact same 3.5-inch touchscreen, that physical size reduction has to mean smaller bezels.

The software experience on the Edge 1060 also sees some updates with an eye on streamlining ride preparation and on-the-road navigation. Garmin has refined the interface by adding a QWERTY keyboard, a new staging checklist, and more customizable home screen layouts, allowing riders to easily reorganize widgets and status pages. Beyond the menus, the device introduces smarter routing capabilities. It’s now possible to compare different route options based on metrics like elevation or bike type, preview upcoming road hazards and traffic before starting, or use the “Free Flow” setting to prioritize paths with the fewest stops and intersections to maintain speed during training efforts. If coffee rides are more your thing, “Up Ahead” notifications will flag approaching points of interest like cafes or restrooms.

If an $800 bike computer is not on your list of future purchases, Garmin is also updating the brand’s lower-priced options that are aimed at riders who want simpler ride tracking and routing features. The Edge Explore 3 is landing at $399.99 while the Edge Explore 3 Plus adds a built-in speaker and microphone, the same as in the Edge 1060, for an extra $100. For those who are comparing, that matches up with the Edge 550 at $499.99, but the Explore series offers a larger screen with touch functionality in exchange for performance-focused details such as smart fueling alerts, electronic groupset integration, and advanced training metrics like real-time stamina and power guide. The Explore series also offers many of the same new routing features found on the flagship 1060, including community-reported road hazard alerts, point-of-interest notifications, and the ability to drop a location pin directly from Apple or Google Maps on a smartphone to immediately generate a bike-specific route. This series is also catered to commuters with Shimano and Bosch e-bike system integrations to display current assist levels and battery life, alongside a new tracking profile that calculates the real-time carbon savings of a given ride. Battery life for the Edge Explore series is quoted as up to 14 hours of demanding use for Explore 3 Plus, while the base Explore 3 stretches that to 16 hours.

The final launch today is a look ahead to the coming winter. The Tacx Nēra is an all-new entry that drops the price of technology significantly with some trickle-down efficiencies. While it’s hardly cheap at $999.99, this is really a budget version of the $1,999.99 Tacx Neo 3M.…

title: Carrick insists Manchester United board back him after Ten Hag points to ‘toxic culture’
author: Jamie Jackson in Como
text:
Ten Hag says Ronaldo did not complete post-match run

Former manager claims club broke promises made to him

Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo “let the team down” during their time together at Manchester United. Ten Hag has also alleged that promises made by United’s owners went unfulfilled, leading to his sacking by the club in October 2024 .

Ronaldo returned for a second spell at United in August 2021 and was already at the club when Ten Hag was appointed in April 2022 as Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s successor . The relationship between the pair quickly broke down, however, with Ronaldo refusing to come on as a substitute in a win against Tottenham in October 2022 before he then publicly criticised the club in a TV interview . The forward’s contract was mutually terminated the following month.

“He let the team down, and he let me down, because we planned with him,” Ten Hag said in an interview with the Athletic. “He’s one of the best in football history. I respected him a lot. But at that time, as a manager, I had to make a rational decision and keep the players I admire in.”

Ten Hag claims Ronaldo did not complete the full run that players were set after they were beaten 4-0 by Brentford early in his reign . “I confronted him with this,” Ten Hag said. “Many times I say: ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score.’”

Ten Hag was sacked only five months after he won the FA Cup and then signed a contract extension. The Dutchman claimed in the discussions with the club’s owners about his new deal that he was made promises which were not kept, and he was left “embarrassed” when Scott McTominay was sold to Napoli without his consent. He said: “They promised me loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep.

“I said: ‘No selling Scott McTominay.’ And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed.”

title: 'She has the engine, and she has the instincts' - Bodine Vollering steps up to the WorldTour with EF Education-Oatly
author: kirsten.frattini@futurenet.com (Kirsten Frattini)
text:
Bodine Vollering is set to step up to the WorldTour with EF Education-Oatly starting in 2025. The Dutch rider aims to continue her development after spending two seasons with the ProTeam VolkerWessels Cycling Team.

“I talked with Esra. The way she spoke about the vision of the team, the way she selected this group of riders, what she’s trying to achieve with them is all to get the best possible results. It’s not just taking a rider and then replacing her after two years. The team has long-term goals, and how they approach everything is really nice. With these conversations, wow, it really woke something in me,” Vollering said.

“And then I see the videos on YouTube. I see how they incorporate fun and how they have a balance between fun and achieving results. I think it’s a really nice environment.”

Vollering said she connected with the EF Education-Oatly team at Classic Lorient Agglomération , where she applauded their strategy and teamwork during the one-day top-tier event.

“I raced Plouay, and I saw the girls from EF Education-Oatly,” she said. “They were controlling the peloton. I saw how strong they were and I thought, wow, because Plouay is a long race. They were in control all day. That’s really amazing, and to be part of such a team, such a community, is exciting.”

This year Vollering was sixth at Festival Elsy Jacobs, and she has finished in the top 10 at Tour de Feminin and Region Pays de la Loire Tour. General Manager Esra Tromp said the team is looking forward to supporting her development in cycling.

"She has the engine, and she has the instincts. She knows the sport inside and out. But she has never had the luxury of being able to dedicate herself completely to racing and training, nor has she had the full range of resources and support to see how far she can go. We can provide that,” Esra said.

Vollering outlined her early experiences with riding as a child with her family but says that she prioritised high school as she got older. She says that following her sister Demi Vollering's career through two overall victories at the Tour de France and a recent win at the World Championships has inspired her.

"I got into cycling, and I did some races, but then when I was in high school, I had a lot going on, so I didn’t race anymore," she said.

"Later, with my sister Demi [winner of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes and world championships], I watched her races, and it really started the fire within me. I wanted to get back on a bike. I wanted to race again. I wanted to see where I could get.”

During the last two seasons, Vollering has split her time between cycling and studying to become a tax lawyer. After completing her thesis, she will focus solely on racing.

“I came to law, and then with my background in high school, I ended up in tax law. That was before I knew I was going to be a cyclist. Now I only have my thesis left to do. It’s exciting because from next year on, for the first time I will be a real cyclist. I can focus on cycling all the way, instead of always having to be exhausted because I have to study, and that's mentally exhausting," she said.

She said that while she enjoys long climbs, she believes the punchy race parcours suit her ability better. Her main goal in her first season with EF Education-Oatly will be to settle in with the team and play a support role for her teammates.

“To be realistic, my main goal for next year is to work for my teammates, and see how I can help them and learn from them the best I can. I think that's really nice to do. My big dream for the future, I dream of the Tour de France. Every year when I watch it gives me goosebumps. I want to be there one day. And also the classics. Amstel Gold because it’s the one big race in the Netherlands,” she said.

title: 'I don't want to be just going through the motions' – Lachlan Morton in search of even more freedom as he departs EF Education to go it alone
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
It was back in 2013 that Lachlan Morton , a young WorldTour professional with Garmin Sharp, set out on an adventure with his brother that spawned the Thereabouts series. That series set the Australian on a path that would eventually send him wildly deviating from the life as a professional cyclist he had once envisaged for himself and fully embracing the opportunity to run an alternate calendar at EF Pro Cycling.

Now, after eight years pushing the pedals in the pink kit of the team from the United States, the rider who has won Unbound 200, set a record time around Australia and captured the imagination with his Alt Tour of the Tour de France is branching out on his own. He confirmed his departure to earlier this month.

Morton's last race with the team was the brutally tough 61km Three Peaks Cyclo-cross in the United Kingdom – which he won – at the end of September and then he quickly set off on his final adventure with the squad. That was his effort to beat the 160-year-old 1,998-mile (3,217-kilometre) horseback record across the American West with his own set of steel steeds, and it was a feat he well and truly pulled off as he eclipsed the six-day 21 hours and 15 minute mark by 19 hours and 45 minutes .

It wasn't exactly a pre-mediated plan to deliver such a jam-packed final send-off to the EF colours,

"It just worked out like that," said Morton of piling the two very different efforts into a narrow window. "But I'm glad it did because it kind of felt like those two events sum up my time with the team pretty nicely.

"Combining a three-hour race with a week-long push, is like it's been in my time with the team. I've combined a lot of different disciplines and elements of racing, and I've always enjoyed that kind of challenge."

It also harked back to the time when Morton's adventures were his own, not under the guise of a team but in the case of the Thereabouts enterprises, a shared endeavour with his brother Angus.

It was important to Morton that he was there to capture this pivotal career moment too, in fact that was reason for the late-season position of the ride dubbed the 'Pony Express'. The timeline needed to be pushed a little later than originally envisaged because his filmmaker brother had welcomed a daughter into the world a couple of months ago, in what is proving to be an era of new beginnings for the siblings.

Early deviations – 'I'm sure that they were not stoked'

It's a little hard to imagine Morton as anything but the multidiscipline adventurer now, but there was a time when he couldn't even conceive of the path that he ended up following with EF Pro Cycling. After all, what was on show at the time he was starting out was a far narrower version of what you had to deliver to be able to ride your bike every day and call it a job.

"I was very much a road racer, and all my my goals were to succeed and win races and do as much as I could in the WorldTour, and then that sort of started to shift," Morton told . "The more I was exposed to it, I guess I started to gradually follow the other passions in cycling and that was sort of happening outside of racing.

"But I never dreamed that I'd be able to race and follow those kind of passions, simultaneously or under one banner. Initially, it was definitely just kind of like a hobby, it was not very closely in line with with what I was doing for a job. I didn't think that the kind of set-up I've had at EF would ever be something that that I could actually do."

It certainly wasn't the norm for a WorldTour professional to go and spend his off season riding 2,500km to Uluru and filming the adventure along the way. But back then, a young Morton didn't really care to do the expected, and that was probably a good thing.

"I was pretty stubborn, and I would just do the things I was going to do anyway," said Morton when asked what the Garmin Sharp team thought when he embarked on the first of three Thereabouts adventures in 2013, with the next two in the Colorado Rocky Mountains and Colombia in the following three years. "So I don't think I really took notice of what people thought, you know. I think the film led reassessing a little bit what I was doing racing."

"I think around that period of time, in my second year with the team, I wasn't racing particularly well, I wasn't particularly happy, and I think in that time I was definitely pretty self-absorbed," said a frank Morton, who isn't afraid to lean into a bit of typical Aussie self deprecation.

"So I don't think I really cared too much what anyone thought, just like a typical like 20-year-old, 21-year-old who is trying to work things out. So yeah, I actually haven't really thought about what they thought. I'm sure that they were not stoked. Maybe, I remember my coach wasn't super happy about it."

Fast forward a few years to the EF Pro Cycling team that formed out of the shell of that original squad, and there was a wholly different attitude. In 2019 Morton, after his sojourn with Jelly Belly and Dimension Data – decided to head back to a set up which was now far more enthused about embracing the unconventional.

It was, in fact, a move he made even though at that point he was quite content in the WorldTour.

"With Dimension Data, I found that as a professional. I was like, 'OK, I found a nice groove here where I can be happy in my life, training and doing this thing and accept the level that'll get me," said Morton.

But the lure of alternative plan was too hard to pass up.

"I remember speaking with some friends of mine at Rapha at the time, and they sort of mentioned the possibility of this idea," said Morton. "Initially, there wasn't any team really attached to it, and still I committed to doing it, which at the time felt sort of risky because it didn't really exist at that time, and cycling, I think, was even more traditional at that time.

"So there was a slight worry about if I was able to do this thing. And then if it doesn't work, if it could be hard to be taken seriously after that. I also didn't know physically, when I started to do longer distance stuff, how that would affect my ability to race. I don't think anyone really knew at that time, but it was just too good of an opportunity, and there were too many things that I realised that I wanted to do other than just road racing, so I was like, 'OK, let's go for it'."

All in on the alternative calendar

Initially while at EF Pro Cycling, Morton combined his alternative calendar with stints of racing with the WorldTour team "as needed". However, as time progressed and Covid came and went, dropping that made more and more sense, particularly with the build in level that meant ducking into the pro road peloton less than ideally prepared was a huge challenge.

"As a rider, I've never had biggest engine, so I need to show up really prepared generally, especially in in that kind of racing," said Morton, who didn't have the room for the type of preparation required given the alternate schedule commitments.

"It was very hard to do the job I needed to do at the race, but also mentally to just like show up and get your head kicked in. So yeah, it just no longer made sense to me to be doing that, especially when it's like there's 18-year-olds who are knocking on the door that deserved that spot more than I did."

By that time, however, there was no doubt of the value of the alternative calendar with the 'Alt Tour' in 2021 a validating experience that capture the public's imagination and showed that "if you do things a little bit outside the box, there's still space for it, it still exists alongside the traditional path," explained Morton.

That and his latest adventure, inspired by an affinity for the courage and tradition of the Pony Express riders that delivered mail through the harsh terrain, were two of the memorable moments he picked out from his time with the team when we spoke to him in the days following the conclusion of his last adventure under its umbrella.

"That was really, really satisfying, from the the group of people I had there and then the route itself, and then the way I was able to ride it. That was a dream one for me, and also to be so removed from cycling in a way, the route itself, it's not one that's been ridden a lot," said Morton.

"It was also cool to get to a point where you could say to the team, 'Hey, I want to do this', and there wasn't a huge amount of questioning about it. There was a trust."

That trust, and evident satisfaction that comes through from Morton when discussing his time with the team raises on big question. Why is he leaving?

"Above everything, I think it's just time is probably the biggest reason," said Morton. "I also don't want to be just going through the motions, knowing I can just do this thing that that works for everyone and just kind of be comfortable in doing that.

"The sport has changed very dramatically, I would say, in the last seven years that I've been with the team, and the the focus that is needed on performance I think is pretty drastic. I just don't see myself fitting in with that really anymore."

So where does he see himself fitting and what are his plans now?

"I think there's some even longer rides I would like to do, and being able to have complete flexibility in my calendar, there's space to be like, 'OK, yes I can go on a ride for like six weeks here' which I'm really excited for," he said.

"I'm also excited to have time to go to specific places and dive into the cycling culture that exists there and learn in a way. Without going into the specifics of routes and places, I think there's a lot of learning I know I'm going to have to do and I'm excited for that."

Still, many things will also be similar, as while Morton says he is well aware of the benefits of the support he gets from the squad, he has put together a good group to fill some of those gaps. Plus the plan is to continue on the path of chasing a mix of races – with Leadville among his goals – and challenges that motivate him. There will, however, perhaps be more of an emphasis on the travel and exploration side of riding, much like where it all began with Thereabouts.

"I've had a lot of a lot of freedom," said Morton of his time with EF. "There hasn't been a lot of compromise on what I would like to do but I just think I'm interested to see where I end up with it, and the things I can do without that kind of attachment and also without the safety net.

"As a 34-year-old man, that has grown up in teams since I was 18 years old, I think it's time for me to get out there by myself."

title: 'Maybe I'll take up gravel' - Still seeking a 2027 contract, Taco van der Hoorn weighs his future
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
After a season full of setbacks and his contract with Lotto-Intermarché coming to an end, Taco van der Hoorn is uncertain whether he will be in the pro peloton in 2027, according to .

The 32-year-old made his reputation as one of the most aggressive riders in the bunch, and his breakaways paid off with a Giro d'Italia stage win in 2021 and a handful of one-day race victories.

However, he was sidelined for most of two seasons after a crash in the 2023 Tour of Flanders left him with severe concussion symptoms . He made his return late in 2024, going on to win the Elfstedenrace, but his last two years have been riddled with illness and injury, which can make contract negotiations difficult.

"At the moment, I actually have no idea what I'm going to do next year," Van der Hoorn said. "There is still a possibility that I will stay with my current team, but it is also possible that I will have to leave. There is also contact with other teams, but that is far from concrete at the moment. So it could go in any direction. It is quite possible that I will still be riding in the WorldTour next year, but it is also possible that I won't be able to find a team at all."

Teams have already had to file their paperwork, including rider contracts to the UCI for the coming season, but there is still time for riders out of contract to find teams before January. Van der Hoorn says his chances of finding a team are fifty-fifty.

"It could just turn out the right way, but it could also just not ... There are still a lot of good riders available on the market for many teams. That makes it difficult. I would really like to continue, because I still enjoy training, racing, and professional life immensely. The difficult thing is that you don't have it entirely in your own hands."

A litany of physical problems, including knee surgery in February and then compensatory pain in the other knee, ruined his spring. Then, just as he was getting back to his top form, another setback hit.

"In Poland, I was really good again. I was part of breakaways and noticed that I was starting to ride at my old level again. That was a huge relief. I regained the confidence that I could still fight for a win this year. And then I crashed again."

His fall in the Renewi Tour left him with a broken hand and elbow, but he still geared up for a return in October, closing out his season at the Eneco Tour.

"It wasn't easy mentally to get myself there again," he said. "But I wanted to try one more time. Of course, I felt the urge to prove myself. I wanted to show that I am still good enough."

Van der Hoorn believes he still has more to give to the sport, like controlling breakaways for a team leader, mentoring young riders or even taking up a completely different sport.

"Suppose it doesn't work out to stay in the WorldTour or as a pro on the road at all, then I could also take up gravel. There are no concrete plans for that yet, but it is something I aspire to. I just really still enjoy cycling and have a competitive mindset. Moreover, I could combine that well with finishing my studies."

Van der Hoorn studied exercise science and is currently pursuing a degree in psychology.

"I think that with my studies and ten years of experience as a pro, I have quite a strong CV to get started somewhere in sports. For example, as a trainer or mentoring young riders. But I don't have any concrete plans for that yet. If I don't manage to find a contract, it could just as easily be that I take a year off and focus entirely on my studies. I wouldn't mind that at all.

"If it ultimately doesn't work out, then so be it. For now, I still hope that I can continue my career as a professional cyclist. I am open to any adventure that comes my way."

Belgian climber makes rare switch from Soudal-QuickStep to Lotto-Intermarché
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The 27-year-old has been with QuickStep since turning pro in 2021 and has three wins to his name – the 2021 GP Industria e Artigianato, a mountain stage of the 2023 Tour of Oman, and a stage of the 2024 Tour of Luxembourg.

This year, he finished seventh at Amstel Gold Race and was fifth from the break on stage 12 of the Vuelta a España. He's moving to Lotto, the team his father, Wim Vansevenant, rode for between 2003 and 2008.

" Lotto-Intermarché is a team with so much history. Over the years, so many talented riders and team leaders have come through its ranks. For me, that's the best proof of the quality of the work being done here," Vansevenant said.

"That's a team I want to be part of. I see my future here. I believe just as strongly in the team's character as I do in the project itself.

"It's not about being part of a huge organisation, but about that family atmosphere. I could already see during the season that there's a really good atmosphere within the team, and I know that's when I can get the very best out of myself."

Riders moving between the two biggest Belgian teams is a relatively rare sight. Pascal Eenkhorn went the other way last year, while Philippe Gilbert's 2019 switch to Lotto was the second-most recent transfer between the two. Looking back another three years, Nikolas Maes and Laurens De Plus went in opposite directions.

Vansevenant is the 10th rider on the incoming list for Lotto next year as their roster gets a major makeover.

French climber Guillaume Martin heads the additions, while Colombian sprinter Juan Sebastián Molano is also joining the team. Meanwhile, homegrown stars Arnaud De Lie and Lennert van Eetvelt move elsewhere.

Vansevenant said he's looking forward to a new challenge with Lotto, noting that he hopes to win a Grand Tour stage while also targeting the Classics.

"Having something new to prove is always a good thing in a career. I've been around for quite a while now.

"I still believe that winning a stage in a Grand Tour is within my capabilities," he said.

"And of course, the Ardennes Classics remain a major priority for me. The Amstel Gold Race, Liège-Bastogne-Liège … Along with the Tour of the Basque Country and other races at that level. Those are the races where I still want to achieve results.

"At the same time, after seven years at the highest level, I'm also more than happy to support the younger generation at Lotto-Intermarché. I know how to position myself in the peloton and how races unfold. I'm happy to pass on that knowledge. I think that's how we can make each other stronger."

Team CEO Jean-François Bourlart praised Vansevenant's offensive racing style, calling him an "important addition" to the squad and saying he can also help the team's younger climbers, such as Jarno Widar.

"With his attacking style of racing, Mauri is a perfect fit for our team. He will be an important addition to our roster, particularly in the Ardennes Classics. He has already proven his qualities in those races over the past few years," he said. "We are convinced that he can take further steps and achieve strong results within our team."

"At the same time, he brings valuable experience to our young group of climbers. We don't just develop talented riders; we also surround them with experienced riders who can help them take the next step. Mauri will play an important role in that process."

title: 32-inch Gravel Gains Steam with New Tires from Continental and Rene Herse
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
In anticipation of next year, when many brands are rumored to be launching 32-inch gravel bikes, two new tires fit for that new wheel standard have been announced. Over the past week, both Continental and Rene Herse announced they will be releasing 32-inch gravel tires in April 2027.

At Big Sugar, Continental unveiled its new 32-inch Dubnital tire that will launch in April. The tire is virtually unchanged from the 700c Dubnital and adds size optionality to the 32-inch width spectrum.

The Rene Herse Indiana Pass will also add to the same category with a 55mm semi-slick option, despite the brand’s CEO’s skepticism of the viability of the new wheel size.

While the Dubnital is the first move to big tires from Continental, this is very much the beginning of a broader push.

Considering the comments the brand has made in it’s soft launch of the 32-inch Dubnital, Continental will add to that 32-inch catalog soon, but on the initial run it will be just the 50mm version of the brand’s popular gravel and cross-country tread.

The Dubnital 32-inch will be available in the race-rapid compound and casing configuration, Continental’s fastest setup for its gravel and mountain bike tires, and is slated to be one of the few 50mm, 32-inch gravel tires.

“The growing interest in 32” wheels is clear, and our priority is ensuring riders have immediate access to Continental’s flagship tire technologies as new wheel sizes emerge,” said Alexander Haenke, Product Manager for MTB & Gravel at Continental Tires. “Choosing the Dubnital as our first 32” release allows us to support evolving setup preferences and frame designs right out of the gate.”

Continental told Velo that the reason why the Dubnital is the first 32-inch gravel tire from the brand is because of its similarity to the 32-inch mountain bike tires the German brand had been working on.

Speaking to professionals in the industry, 32-inch gravel tires are lagging behind the mountain bike tires because R&D from the big brands on 32-inch gravel began much later than 32-inch mountain bike tech. Interestingly, come next year, when many of these 32-inch bikes start to roll out, there might be more gravel options than mountain bikes.

The Dubnital 32-inch 50mm tire will be a key addition to the market because when those gravel bikes start to roll out, there are not tons of great gravel-sized tire options.

Similarly, Rene Herse has also announced 32-inch tires that will enter the 50-55mm width market to meet the anticipated demand that will come from the new bikes. The Rene Herse Indiana Pass, named after the high point of the Tour Divide, uses the Rene Herse semi-slick tread, will come in four different constructions, and will be available in 55mm.

Rene Herse is a notable entry into the 32-inch tire game because Jan Hiene, the brand’s CEO, has been a vocal opponent of the bigger wheel size. He was so vociferous in this stance that we hosted a debate between Heine and John Karrasch, one of 32-inch wheels most vocal proponents of 32-inch wheels, on the Velo podcast .

The flip from the brand doesn’t seem to be a change of opinion. Instead, it was a response to requests from Rene Herse’s professional athletes to have tires to support the new bikes they will be riding in 2027. In particular, the tires will support Meaghan Hackinen, the 2026 Tour Divide winner who will race the Salsa Fargo 32 next year, and gravel pros Ted King and Brennan Wertz.

“Both Ted and Brennan are tall and very strong riders, so they are perfect candidates to benefit from the larger wheels,” Jan Heine said in the press release. “They are curious about the new wheel size, but they don’t want to give up the speed, comfort and grip of their supple Rene Herse semi-slicks. That’s why we’ll offer their favorite tires in the 32-inch size.”

Neither of these tires are available yet, as both tires are set to roll out in April.

title: Jayco, Picnic Confirm WorldTour Plans for 2027 Despite Registration Hiccups
author: ahood
text:
Officials from both Picnic-PostNL and Jayco-AlUla confirmed they are still seeking WorldTour licenses in 2027. (Photo: Getty Images)

Jayco-AlUla and Picnic-PostNL say they are preparing for the 2027 WorldTour season despite missing the UCI’s first registration deadline , officials from both teams confirmed to Velo .

So far, it’s just paperwork, with a bank guarantee delay and an unresolved equipment partnership holding up their applications.

Both organizations explained their absence from the UCI’s initial registration lists published Monday. The omissions affect their men’s and women’s WorldTour programs.

Neither has been refused registration, because both have time to complete their files before the UCI publishes its final list December 8.

Jayco’s parent organization, GreenEDGE Cycling, said the delay impacting Jayco-AlUla and Liv AlUla Jayco is due to an international banking procedure.

“We are aware that Team Jayco AlUla and Liv AlUla Jayco’s names are absent from the recent UCI teams registration list,” a press note read.

“This is purely due to a technical transfer process that will be resolved very soon. Processing the bank guarantee required by the UCI involves cross-border financial operations that sometimes can encounter delays.”

GreenEDGE said preparations for next season continue for the Aussie-backed team that’s been in the peloton since 2012. Daniel Benson has reported a new title partner is coming online, but so far, there is no official confirmation.

“We can confirm that GreenEDGE Cycling’s planning and preparation for the 2027 season remains on track and we looking forward to racing our 16th season in the WorldTour,” officials said.

Picnic-PostNL said its outstanding paperwork concerns a technical partnership following the bankruptcy of its current partner’s company.

The team recently made headlines following a report of a toxic team environment , something several staffers and riders denied.

The team did not identify the technical partner in its statement or give a date for completing the agreement.

“Our Men and Women’s programs are currently in the application process for WorldTour status in the coming year,” a statement read. “To this end, the team still needs to provide information relating to the finalization of a partnership with a technical partner for the coming season, following the bankruptcy of the current partner’s company. We will be doing this in the coming period.”

Despite a rough 2026 season , the statement confirms that Picnic-PostNL will be pursuing WorldTour status.

There were some suggestions from a source that told Velo that the team might step down to a ProTeam license in 2027, but the team’s statement Tuesday suggests it intends to remain at the WorldTour.

The explanations came after the UCI’s October 15 deadline for applicants to submit essential registration documents.

If both teams see their paperwork filed and in order, that will mean that 18 men’s and 14 women’s teams will race at the top-level WorldTour category in 2027.

Those licenses are important because it gives team automatic invitations to the team’s most important stage races and one-day classics, including the Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes.

Missing the initial deadline does not prevent teams from securing registration, although it can carry consequences for rider contracts.

“In accordance with the UCI Regulations and subject to other applicable provisions, riders from these teams may terminate their contracts early, but this right will lapse if their team is subsequently registered,” the UCI stated.

Ben O’Connor is leaving Jayco-AlUla for Decathlon CMA-CGM in a move confirmed Tuesday, but that deal was signed months ago and was a result of the team’s filing delay, sources said.

There are another few tidbits in the team registry.

Modern Adventure Factor Racing appears among the men’s ProTeam applicants, confirming earlier reports that Factor would be joining the George Hincapie project for 2027 and beyond as a co-sponsor .

Soudal also loses Quick-Step as a co-title sponsor and will be called Soudal-Safety Jogger for 2027, making an end of an era for the Belgian flooring company.

Quick-Step was either title or co-sponsor of the team since its founding in 2003, and co-sponsor of Mapei from 1999 to 2002. The company will remain a partner backer of the team.

title: Why Does an Event Like BorderLands Gravel Matter?
author: Kelly Matkovich
text:
The Arizona borderlands is a geographic and cultural region on the northern side of the Arizona-Mexico border. To talk about the borderlands area as a whole transcends the line on the map and is where the two countries meet.

While the topic of the border has been hotly contested in the current political environment, the history of the border shows it’s not only been complicated, but the border itself has moved. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the Mexican-American War in 1848. As a result, the United States purchased land that is now California, Nevada, Utah, and parts of Arizona and New Mexico. Five years later came the Gadsden Purchase, where the U.S. added even more land, which includes where Douglas, Arizona, sits today. While Douglas wasn’t officially incorporated until 1905, that meant if you lived in the area, you went to bed in Mexico, and the next day, you woke up, and the land was now part of the United States.

It’s complicated and yet beautiful at the same time.

This paints the backdrop for the BorderLands Gravel race , which starts and finishes in the border town of Douglas. Sure, it would’ve been easy to start writing about the race itself, focusing on the course, the mileage, podium winners, and more. However, once the racers left the pavement a short distance outside of town, the gravel road veered south, and the most prominent feature right before our eyes was the Arizona-Mexico border wall. It’s about context. Sitting just about 4,000 feet in elevation, Douglas exists in the transitional zone between the Sonoran and Chihuahuan Deserts. Now in its third year, BorderLands Gravel returns to Douglas on November 14, 2026.

One of the questions surrounding the event for me was this: why does an event like BorderLands Gravel matter? Along with that, other questions pop up. What impact does a gravel race in Douglas have? What value or benefit does it bring to the community? Also, why did racers travel, in some cases, great distances to ride and race this stretch of desert gravel roads along the border?

As to why this matters for the community of Douglas, we need to first look at some data.

According to the “2024 Outdoor Participation Trend Report” by the Outdoor Foundation and the Outdoor Industry Association, “In 2023, the outdoor recreation participant base grew 4.1% to a record 175.8 million participants: 57.3% of all Americans aged six and older” (p. 3). Americans continue to get outside to recreate. Even more so, of the 175.8 million participants in outdoor recreation, 17.2% of them recreated on a bicycle. That number equates to 30+ million Americans enjoying the outdoors by bike.

At the same time, as more people recreate outdoors, it is having a positive economic impact. Outdoor adventuring consumers spend $887 billion annually. That results in 7.6 million jobs, $65.3 billion in federal tax revenue, and $59.2 billion in state and local tax revenue. In Arizona, consumers spend $21.2 billion on outdoor recreation, which funds 201,000 jobs, $5.7 billion in wages and salaries, and $1.4 billion in state and local tax revenue.

Lastly, as it pertains specifically to gravel cycling, it has been experiencing an explosion of growth. Not only are innumerable bike brands creating whole lines of gravel-specific bicycles, but races and events like BorderLands Gravel are on the rise. According to BikeReg’s 2025 year-end data , gravel race registrations have grown more than tenfold since 2015, far outpacing mountain bike, road, cyclocross, and recreational events. Simply put, more people are enjoying the outdoors on gravel bikes.

For communities across Arizona, there’s an impetus to strategically and thoughtfully tap into the resource of capturing spending on outdoor recreation. That’s why events like BorderLands Gravel matter for a community like Douglas.

While Douglas has a stable employment base due to its shared border with Agua Prieta, one of the challenges is its rural location. However, where some see challenges or even weaknesses, others see opportunities. Suppose you’re going to host a gravel cycling race. In that case, you need some basic agreements that Douglas has in abundance … miles of gravel roads, stunning desert scenery, mild temperatures, the City of Douglas staff on board, and innumerable stakeholders, agencies, and landowners linking arms to make the race happen. In other words, the whole community was on board and behind it. Even more so, you need a visionary spearheading the event and tethering together all of these pieces and relationships. That’s why race organizer Mike Miller is the straw that stirs this drink.

However, it’s more than the economic impact; it’s about showcasing the community of Douglas and the beautiful surrounding landscape.

As Mike Miller dreamed of this event, Douglas became the unexpected destination for a premier gravel cycling event, thanks to the storied Gadsden Hotel. Inspired by the hotel’s historic charm, the vision for a gravel bike race on the iconic Geronimo Trail began to take shape. The process kicked off in November 2023, with a meeting between Mike and the Gadsden Hotel’s General Manager, followed by discussions with local tourism and city officials. By January 2024, the concept had gained official backing, setting the stage for an event that would showcase Douglas’s rich heritage and rugged terrain.…

My Death Valley Heat Training Failed Miserably. Here Is What I Learned.
author: Josh Ross
text:
In 2024, I rode 1,000km from Reno to Las Vegas, with the big draw being a chance to cruise through Death Valley. What sounded great on paper turned into 30 mph headwinds and temperatures up to 110°F (43°C). On the 3,000-foot climb out of the valley, I could only manage about 500 feet of elevation at a time before collapsing under a scrubby bush for 10 minutes to rest and regroup. Needless to say, I was looking for redemption.

I wanted another crack at the desert adventure, but I certainly didn’t want to relive that heat horror, so I decided to try heat training. It’s essentially repeated exposure to enough heat stress to force your body to adapt. For more scientific insight, I reached out to Brian Maiorano, Coach Liaison at CORE Body Temperature, to find out what’s actually happening inside your body during the process.

“When you consistently cause the body stress by raising your heat strain index, it says, hey, I don’t like this. This is causing me more work,” Maiorano explained. “Your body then adapts by creating more blood plasma. And that extra blood plasma is what allows you to start sweating earlier and start sweating more profusely.”

It’s that increased plasma volume that gives you a more effective sweat response, helping your body better manage the physiological stress of exercising in the heat. Sounds ideal. So how do you actually do it?

I don’t own a bike trainer. I’m the type of cyclist who would ride through a hurricane before I sit on a hamster wheel. (Spoiler alert: we did hit the tail end of a hurricane in the desert, but more on that later). So when it came to heat training, my only option was outside. My inspiration was that now-iconic social media video of Tom Pidcock heat training for Worlds , so I basically recreated it. I wore a full wool winter kit, topped with a CORE Body Temperature Tyvek suit. Over that, I added a Rapha down jacket with the hood up, plus thick restaurant freezer gloves—the kind you saw Jonas Vingegaard using at the fish factory. I added sweat shorts over the Tyvek suit to help block the wind, winter shoe covers, a wool cap, my puffy hood, and finally my helmet.

It was giving Beastie Boys in the “Intergalactic” music video. I looked absolutely deranged. I was also hot, and that was the goal. I used this setup to bike outside three times a week for three weeks, and each session lasted one to two hours.

According to Maiorano, the strategy I had in mind was possible. “You can do it on a road bike,” he says, but the focus needs to be getting “your layering more dialed in to prevent the wind evaporation.” In other words, the challenge isn’t necessarily creating enough heat; it’s keeping your body from getting rid of it. On a road bike, the constant airflow helps sweat evaporate and cool you, which is exactly what you’re trying to limit. Maiorano explains, “Try a normal cycling kit, but then over top of that, a snug rain jacket and snug rain pants. And then thermal layers on top of the rain jacket. The reason you don’t want the thermal layers underneath is because you’re the one generating the sweat. If you get the thermal layers wet trapped inside the rain jacket, they’ll get soaked and cool you off. So thermal layers on the outside.” You’ll notice, this was my first of many mistakes.

A CORE sensor will certainly do the trick but I started my training block without one. The sensor tracks a metric called a heat strain index, which combines your core temperature and your skin temperature. “The heat strain index goes from 0 to 10,” Maiorano explains. “For heat training, that magic spot is 3 to 7. You just want to get in there and hold that for 45 minutes, 60 minutes, 90 minutes if you’re really looking for an intense session.”

If you don’t have a sensor, Maiorano says he used to tell his athletes to “go cook yourself, but don’t overcook yourself.” The obvious problem: What exactly does that even mean? A sensor gives athletes a target, but over time it can also teach you what an appropriate heat session feels like. Maiorano compares it to riding with a power meter: eventually, you can probably guess your power within a few watts without looking down. Heat training can work the same way.

The honest answer? Not great. My husband Richard was following the same heat-training protocol as I was. In fact, he even had hotter weather to train in during an elusive San Francisco summer heat wave while I was travelling. But on day one of our three-day trip, 109 miles into a 160-mile day, he was puking in the bushes with temperatures hitting 109°F. Day two is where the wheels fell off for me.

I was riding in the remnants of Hurricane Rachel, battling a diabolical headwind through Death Valley that had me, Josh Ross, Mike Levy, and other friends doing everything we could to hold 10 mph in a full echelon across the road. After three hours of unrelenting wind, my speed had dropped to 8 mph and I was done. I sat under that well-known Death Valley scrubby bush and tried to regroup. After what felt like an eternity—which was probably only 10 minutes—I got back on my bike and was immediately dizzy, with zero power in my legs. Game over.

Sadly, I didn’t even make it to the 3,000-foot climb out of the valley, which I had originally thought would be the true heat-training test. Instead, I got to test whether my iPhone satellite feature would work to get an SOS text to our friends running SAG. Desert: 1. Lisa: 0.

Was it the heat that actually did me in? According to Maiorano, on an ultra-endurance ride, it’s not that simple. Heat, fatigue, and fueling can compound on each other. Overheating increases cardiovascular strain and can interfere with digestion and fueling, while inadequate fueling can further compromise performance.…

title: These 5 Transfers Will Transform Pro Cycling in 2027
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Grand tour winners, former world champions, and one of USA’s hottest talents will make career-defining transfers this winter.

Richard Carapaz, Giulio Ciccone, Filippo Ganna, Felix Gall, and Andrew “AJ” August are the headline names making moves in a wildly busy transfer window that’s already seen Tom Pidcock get a superteam and Lidl-Trek go transfer crazy.

These five blockbuster moves promise the riders more freedom, leadership opportunities, and career progression. They offer the teams victories from Paris-Roubaix through the Tour de France.

Broken contracts, bizarre motivations, and troubled teams accompany some of these biggest moves of 2026-2027.

Here’s all you need to know about the five biggest transfers in the men’s peloton, as of October 20.

Stay tuned for a similar feature on some whopper contracts in the women’s sport.

For Carapaz: How does Richard Carapaz benefit by moving to NSN Cycling Team?

If you’ve got an answer, please let us know.

This feels like a sideways, or maybe even a backward move for one of the top-ranked riders in the world.

EF Education-EasyPost isn’t the best GC team in the world, but it’s been good enough to put Carapaz into the top-4 of a grand tour for three years in a row. Plus, it allowed its biggest rider the flexibility to roam free. Stage hunting, the KoM classification, GC – nothing was off-limits for Carapaz at EF.

What does NSN have to offer Carapaz (beyond a bigger paycheck)?

The Swiss-registered squad was a sprint-focused team in its debut 2026 season.

It’s bolstered its climbing division with Santiago Buitrago and Lennert Van Eetvelt for 2027, but is still short on the climbing support Carapaz might need if he wants to go big at the Tour de France.

Beyond that, Carapaz might not get such a long leash at an ambitious team that clearly wants to break into GC racing. Here’s hoping he can keep bringing the panache.

For NSN Cycling Team: The answer is obvious – the team gets possibly the most exciting racer in the world. Carapaz will bring the team results, charisma, and guaranteed TV time.

Luring Carapaz from EF was the heist of the season , and by far the biggest transfer in the men’s peloton so far.

Carapaz broke his contract with EF to join NSN.

There’s no rumor of bad blood between the Ecuadorian superstar and the American team that gave him free rein over his racing ambitions. It just supported him through one of the best seasons of his career.

EF boss Jonathan Vaughters confirmed this week to Escape Collective that he’s suffering a budget crunch – something already evident in the exodus of talent leaving the team this winter and its sparse recruitment policy.

Maybe NSN made Carapaz an offer he couldn’t refuse, and one that Vaughters couldn’t match. The likelihood of a buyout fee would have made it a reluctant no-brainer for the impoverished American team.

For Ciccone: Giulio Ciccone will be a great white shark at Pinarello-Q36.5, having been one of many fish in an overflowing pond at Lidl-Trek.

The exuberant Italian will join Tom Pidcock as one of the ultimate bigs at Pinarello-Q36.5, which is rapidly emerging as one of the most audacious, ambitious teams in the bunch.

How Ciccone and Pidcock divide the calendar and their ambitions is another matter. Scheduling two top riders with such similar skill sets won’t be simple.

For Pinarello-Q36.5: Ciccone could have won GP Québec, the European championships, and Il Lombardia in the last month. When combined with Pidcock and Mauro Schmid, Pinarello-Q36.5 will have the ultimate triple-threat on suitably punchy parcours.

And if Pinarello-Q36.5 has Ciccone, Pidcock, and Schmid divide and conquer, they’ll be drowning in the UCI points they need to hit the WorldTour in 2029.

Ciccone was signed with Lidl-Trek through 2029. However, the 31-year-old was reportedly rubbed the wrong way by the recent management overhaul and identity shift at his long-time team. The Italian was a close ally of former team boss Luca Guercilena, who appears to have been squeezed out of his role in the team’s structural upheaval.

The overload of GC racers at Lidl-Trek no doubt improved Cicco’s mood, either.

This seems to have been an ugly divorce. The statements from Ciccone and Lidl-Trek confirming their contract termination couldn’t have been frostier.

For Ganna: Filippo Ganna needed a reboot, bad. The towering Italian has huge potential, and it’s been going untapped.

Sure, Remco Evenepoel is unbeatable against the clock right now, but Ganna’s proven he can be a lot more than just a time trialist. Remember his forays into bunch sprinting? Or his barnstorming breakaway antics at the 2020 Giro?

Aside from his spectacular win at Dwars Door Vlaanderen, Ganna lost his road-racing chops this season.

Ganna must see a move to Lidl-Trek as a new chapter.

New management, new motivation, and a team committed to classics racing and sprinting might restore the true “Top Ganna.”

For Lidl-Trek: Lidl-Trek must have watched the Italian track pursuit team and liked what it saw. Just imagine Ganna leading out his Italian pursuit teammate Jonathan Milan at the Giro d’Italia?! Bellissimo .

Ganna will bring Lidl-Trek a leadout man de-luxe and a heavyweight addition to its already hulking classics squad next year.

Ganna, Milan, Mads Pedersen, and Mathias Vacek could flatten even the most gnarled, off-set cobblestones of Paris-Roubaix. In a race as unpredictable as “The Hell of the North,” this type of full-frontal offense could compensate for Lidl-Trek not having a Pogi, Wout, or Mathieu.

Sadly for Lidl-Trek, multiple second-tier leaders aren’t so advantageous in grand tours, as we’re about to explore …

Ganna split from Netcompany Ineos a year early, and it seems like the British team did little to stop it from happening. According to Domestique , Netcompany Ineos didn’t demand a transfer payment from Lidl-Trek and may have even sweetened the deal.…

Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO
author: Julia Kollewe
text:
Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.

Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.

Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.

Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.

On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.

Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.

The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.

At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.

However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.

It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.

Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.

Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.

“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”
