title: Honda confirms Moreira for factory team in 2027; Alonso heads to LCR
Will Lindblad and Lawson be retained by Racing Bulls? F1 Q&A
text:
Kimi Antonelli has his first opportunity to secure the 2026 drivers' championship at this weekend's United States Grand Prix in Austin.

Antonelli must win the race with Mercedes team-mate George Russell finishing ninth or lower and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton fifth or lower.

Austin is the first of six races scheduled to take place between now and the end of the season in December.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the race in Texas.

Will Liam Lawson get the Racing Bulls seat for next year? - Chris

Racing Bulls are one of only two teams where the 2027 driver line-up is not finalised. The other is Haas, where Oliver Bearman has not yet been confirmed alongside new signing Rafael Camara, although that is only a matter of time.

At Racing Bulls, it's a three-don't-fit-into-two situation, with current race drivers Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad in the frame along with Red Bull junior driver Nikola Tsolov, the Bulgarian who is second in the Formula 2 championship at the moment.

This is the first time in Red Bull history that Helmut Marko is not in charge of driver choice at the junior team and it's unclear what approach they will take under the new management.

In the past, one might have expected them to drop Lawson, on the basis that he has had his chance and is not likely to be considered a long-term candidate for a full-time seat at Red Bull, and put Tsolov in alongside Lindblad.

But there is an argument that the Red Bull young driver programme has been mismanaged for 20 years by Marko and former team boss Christian Horner and they should take a more considered, patient, methodological approach.

In the past, Marko and Horner took a very ruthless approach. A driver would get a shot, and if they did not deliver pretty much immediately, they were dropped.

On one level, it made sense - they were looking for world-class drivers who could lead Red Bull. And if a driver was not that level, they felt they had no use for them.

But at the same time, it sometimes meant putting two unknown quantities together, which made it harder to judge the quality of either.

An alternative approach might be to keep a known-quality benchmark on board against which it is easier to judge the ability of a newcomer.

On that basis, it would make sense to keep Lawson and Lindblad together for 2027 and make Tsolov the reserve, put him in the simulator and give him some tests in older cars to provide him with F1 experience.

The reasoning is that while Lindblad's debut season has been impressive in patches, Lawson is consistently quicker at the moment, both in qualifying and in races.

So if Lindblad is to be considered a future candidate for Red Bull, this argument would go, he should be given an extra season to prove whether he can consistently beat Lawson. Because if he can't, the obvious conclusion is that he is not a candidate for the senior team.

If they put Tsolov in with Lindblad, they have two unknown quantities, which helps no-one in the bigger picture.

A decision has not yet been taken, and ultimately it rests with the shareholders, Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz, with under them Red Bull CEO Oliver Mintzlaff, who is in overall charge of the F1 programme.

Why is F1 going to another country, Rwanda, with what can only be described as very poor human rights? Is this another case of if you have the cash we'll come to your country irrespective of significant international concern regarding the suppression of political dissent, press freedom and the country's military involvement in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo? - Paul

Formula 1's owner Liberty Media has been looking to establish a race in Africa since it took over the sport in 2017.

It was the one glaring omission from the calendar, and the race in Rwanda will give F1 a presence on every single inhabited continent, as well as access to a largely untapped market.

But finding a country that is suitable to be a host has not been easy.

Various possibilities were investigated. There was a project in Morocco near Tangier, but that didn't have the necessary finance.

At one point, F1 looked quite close to a deal to return to Kyalami in South Africa for the first time since 1993, but there were issues with the promoter.

There are currently as many as four separate projects in South Africa, including Kyalami and two in Cape Town. But they are all too far away from being realistic possibilities.

Many - if not most - grands prix are funded by governments in one way or another, so it's hardly a surprise that the one African bid to come to fruition has government backing.

It's a sensitive situation because Rwanda receives international aid, and the government and F1 have been keen to emphasise that the funding is coming from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment.

Then there are the accusations of 'sportswashing' - a term given to the use of major sports events to distract from aspects of the country's conduct that parts of the wider international community find problematic.

Rwanda is the subject of a case brought by its neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.

DRC's Minister of Foreign Affairs Therese Kayikwamba Wagner issued a statement last week to say that while DR Congo supported the idea of a grand prix in Africa, they were opposed to Rwanda being its host.

She accused Rwanda President Paul Kagame of "fuelling a devastating war in our country", adding that wars in the DRC have claimed millions of lives, that people continue to be driven from their homes and Congolese natural resources exploited and appropriated.…

title: Specialized and Quick-Step End One of the Most Important Partnerships in Pro Cycling
author: Jim Cotton
text:
(Photo: Tim de Waele/Corbis via Getty Images))

Specialized bikes and team Quick-Step officially ended one of the most significant partnerships in road racing Monday.

Both the U.S. bike behemoth and the long-running Belgian team confirmed Monday the end of an 18-year collaboration that brought the so-called “Wolf Pack” more than 800 victories.

Beginning in 2007, the partnership put the Specialized logo on top of the biggest races in the world and helped develop some of the most popular road bikes on the market.

The split marks the end of an era in professional cycling.

The collaboration between the brand and the team was one of the longest, most successful partnerships in the peloton.

Quick-Step riders won cobblestone monuments, Tour de France stages, and world titles on various iterations of the Tarmac, Shiv, and Venge. Riders like Tom Boonen, Mark Cavendish, and Remco Evenepoel are among the superstars who forged their palmarés on the brand’s bikes.

In return, the team helped Specialized refine some of its most successful models sold to the mass market .

Cavendish and Evenepoel are known to have been particularly active in developing its sprint and TT bikes, respectively.

The collaboration began in 2007, paused in 2010 and 2011, and has continued since 2012.

The news that the end was nigh was first reported , though not confirmed, in April.

Separate social media posts by both Specialized and Soudal Quick-Step on Monday made it official.

“After nearly two decades together, we’ve celebrated some of the sport’s most iconic moments, including victories in monument classics, grand tours, world championships, and countless stage races,” Specialized wrote on an Instagram post Monday.

“Thank you to the riders, staff, management, and fans who helped make this partnership so memorable and wishes Soudal Quick-Step and AG Insurance-Soudal continued success in the years ahead.”

It will be all change for the team currently known as Soudal Quick-Step in 2027.

The team will ride Merida Bikes and be known as Soudal Safety Jogger.

The Belgian flooring company Quick-Step steps down from its title sponsorship of the team for the first time in 24 years this winter.

Meanwhile, Merida will return to the peloton after it was last seen in 2025 with Bahrain Victorious. The Taiwanese manufacturer owns a 35 percent stake in Specialized.

The partnering women’s team AG Insurance-Soudal will also switch from Specialized to Merida in 2027.

With the Quick-Step team off the books, Specialized will tighten its focus on its ongoing partnerships.

The California-based brand will continue to invest in its partnerships with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, FDJ United-Suez United, SD Worx Protime, and the Specialized Factory Racing off-road superteam .

Demi Vollering, Remco Evenepoel, Keegan Swenson, and Lotte Kopecky will be its biggest-name athletes going forward.

MTB star Kate Courtney will also ride Specialized on the road after she made her bombshell move to FDJ United Suez this summer.

Tim Merlier won Quick-Step’s last race on a Specialized bike Sunday at the Eneco Tour. The Belgian super-sprinter gave his bike an affectionate tap after he blasted across the finishline.

“I think it is my 80th professional victory. I don’t know how many I have achieved on a Specialized [57 – ed], but since I started riding this brand of bikes, I’ve achieved many victories,” Merlier said at the finish Sunday.

“I’m very proud that I can finish this season with a victory for Specialized,” he said.

It was a suitably winning end to one of the winningest, most recognizable partnerships in pro road racing.

title: She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home
author: Niha Masih
text:
​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism

B efore 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.

That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.

“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”

It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.

The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.

I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.

The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out ; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them .

R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.

After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.

Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)

“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”

But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.

“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”

With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.

During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.

Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.

“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.

R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.

Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue .)

R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.

“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.

Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.

It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”…
